Review PR 137

I’m using the GitHub review workflow to inspect PR 137, then I’ll validate the changed code locally and report only actionable findings. I’ll also follow this repository’s graph-first guidance for tracing affected symbols.

PR 137 is a same-repository security fix touching `init-agents`: about 1,300 changed lines across the implementation, tests, and docs. All GitHub build/test jobs are green; the separate Entire gate is failing, so I’m checking both the confinement logic and the failure signal rather than relying on CI alone.

The main risk is in the custom absolute-symlink resolver, not `os.Root` itself. I found a suspicious lexical `filepath.Clean` that may erase an untraversable `..`; I’m running a minimal differential reproduction against the PR head to confirm whether it can still redirect a managed write.
Ok, any changes?

No project source files have been changed—I’m reviewing only. I’ve confirmed two merge-blocking resolver regressions so far: absolute aliases can still redirect a write after lexical `..` cleanup, and terminal `.`/slashes can bypass the filesystem’s directory check. I’m checking whether the PR head moved, then I’ll give you the final review.
You won't show me the content. Can you just fix it?

Yes. I’ll apply the confirmed resolver fixes on a local branch based on PR 137, add regression coverage, and run the focused suite. I’m using the PR-comment fix workflow so the changes stay isolated from your current branch; I won’t post, commit, or push anything without separate authorization.
I don't think this worked?

You’re right—I had only reproduced the bugs in an isolated review worktree, so nothing visible changed in the shared workspace. I’m moving the workspace onto a new `codex/pr-137-fixes` branch based on PR 137 and applying the fixes there now.
The temporary review ref was cleaned up, but the exact PR head commit is still available locally. I’m branching from that immutable commit instead.

The shared workspace is now on the PR-fix branch. I’m patching the resolver so it preserves the filesystem’s raw path semantics instead of cleaning them away, while keeping valid in-project absolute aliases working.
